articles.title: The Rook Board: thirteen kickers, and the question the stopwatch cannot answer
articles.dek: Maractus leads the visible scouting bands. Luvdisc wins the workout. Calvin Rook separates those two arguments, ranks all thirteen kickers and names the clubs that should investigate.
articles.author: calvin-rook

body.text: I can tell you which kicker ran the fastest forty. I cannot tell you which one will make a forty-seven-yard field goal from these numbers. That is the first useful distinction in this week’s Rook Board, and the one I expect somebody to ignore before reaching the third prospect.

Accumula State’s Maractus is my first evaluation because his visible 65–93 scouting band leads the class. University of Fortree’s Luvdisc is the athlete I want to watch longest: 4.71 in the forty, a forty-two-inch vertical and a 6.37 cone. Both judgments can be true. The class contains thirteen visible kickers, two separate Grubbin prospects and no supplied college accuracy chart or measured kicking-distance session. The upper end of a scouting band is not a current ability rating.

The IFL supplies plenty of reasons to take the position seriously. Petalburg’s Sunflora is nine-for-nine on field goals through Week 12. Fortree’s Lanturn is eleven-for-twelve. Fuchsia’s Gorebyss is seven-for-sixteen and Olivine’s Sunflora eight-for-fourteen. Those totals invite different conversations, although distance and circumstances still matter before anybody declares an incumbent finished. Fortree has enough other problems without treating a local college kicker as an automatic solution.

My comparisons below are evaluation fits, not draft orders or claims that a club has committed to change. A sprint can suggest usefulness in coverage. A cone can make an athlete worth examining in space. Neither demonstrates repeatable contact, placement or range. I am ranking the available evidence, then identifying the football question I would ask next. Maractus gets the first appointment; Luvdisc gets the longest second look.

prospects.name: Maractus
prospects.analysis: Accumula State's Maractus goes first because the 65–93 visible scouting band is the highest in this group. The workout is respectable rather than theatrical: 4.95 in the forty, thirteen bench repetitions, thirty-one inches vertically and 6.95 through the cones. At twenty-three and level six, this is a very different development proposition from the more advanced Charjabug below. I want to see actual kicking before turning a promising band into a dependable Sunday leg. The resemblance to Lavender's Just a cactus and Mossdeep's Adam Vinathorn makes a convenient introduction; it does not transfer their results to a college prospect.
prospects.concern: We have no prospect field-goal distances or accuracy chart. Nothing in the forty establishes where his reliable kicking range ends.
prospects.projection: My first kicking evaluation. Fuchsia, with seven makes in sixteen season field-goal attempts, should investigate; that record invites comparison, not a prewritten replacement decision.

prospects.name: Stunfisk
prospects.analysis: Celadon Metropolitan's Stunfisk owns a 63–91 band, close enough to Maractus that I will not pretend the order is a settled verdict. The 5.07 forty and 7.06 cone are unremarkable movement results. They also answer a question a place-kicker is rarely hired primarily to solve. He is twenty-two and level eight, and the next useful evidence would concern his actual striking routine. I would rather admit what this workout does not show than turn a slow cone into a missed forty-yard attempt in my imagination.
prospects.concern: The promising scouting interval remains wide. A twenty-nine-inch jump does not prove a weak leg or a strong one.
prospects.projection: A serious top-of-group alternative for Olivine, whose eight makes in fourteen attempts give Jasmine reason to compare options carefully.

prospects.name: Luvdisc
prospects.analysis: Here is the Hoenn prospect I am going to spend too much time discussing. University of Fortree's Luvdisc ran 4.71, jumped forty-two inches and completed the cone in 6.37, all the best marks in this thirteen-player group. The 59–87 band does not lead the class, but the athlete certainly gets my attention. Those movement results could matter in coverage or an emergency scramble; they still need a football job to justify the admiration. At level twenty-one, he offers a different visible starting point from the two names above him.
prospects.concern: Athleticism cannot substitute for repeatable placement. I am ranking an intriguing evaluation, not certifying him as the class's most accurate kicker.
prospects.projection: Sunyshore should take a close look after four field goals in seven attempts. Fortree should enjoy its local prospect without forgetting Lanturn is already eleven-for-twelve.

prospects.name: Charjabug
prospects.analysis: Ballonlea State's Charjabug is twenty-one, level twenty-four and carries a 60–88 scouting interval. That combination earns fourth even though the 5.09 forty and 7.00 cone will not generate a workout montage. Fifteen bench repetitions distinguish him from the two Grubbin prospects without proving anything specific about ball flight. The relevant attraction is a relatively young player with a more advanced visible level and an encouraging band. Cinnabar and Snowpoint already use Charjabug kickers; those familiar silhouettes should prompt questions about this individual, not a species-wide scouting shortcut.
prospects.concern: Level is a development marker, not a guarantee that his placement or distance is superior to lower-level candidates.
prospects.projection: A priority comparison for Mauville alongside the higher-band options. Sunflora's thirteen-for-nineteen season calls for a careful evaluation of the misses before a roster judgment.

prospects.name: Klawf
prospects.analysis: Levincia Technical's Klawf makes the strongest physical case after Luvdisc: 4.84 in the forty, twenty-two bench repetitions, a thirty-seven-inch vertical and 6.69 cone. That bench result leads the group comfortably. His 56–84 band keeps him below several less spectacular workouts in my order. I am interested in whether the athlete can add useful special-teams work around the central kicking assignment. I am not going to translate twenty-two repetitions into a fictional sixty-yard field goal. He is twenty-two and level eleven, with plenty still to establish.
prospects.concern: The strongest bench performance supplies no direct measurement of kicking power. His upper scouting endpoint is also below the leading candidates.
prospects.projection: Rustboro should include him in a broader specialist comparison; the Stone have used several kickers, and a useful athlete deserves a look without being promised the job.

prospects.name: Grubbin
prospects.analysis: North Kalos University's Grubbin gets the first of the two Grubbin places. He is twenty-two, level fourteen, and carries a 58–86 interval. The 5.04 forty, nine bench repetitions and thirty-five-inch vertical are a little stronger overall than Coumarine Coastal's nearby entry, although the cone comparison reverses by two hundredths. That is a modest ordering judgment, not an enormous football distinction. The school name matters here because the species name alone would collapse two separate prospects into one misleading evaluation.
prospects.concern: The near-identical profiles need kicking evidence to separate them. Small combine differences should not become a large confidence gap.
prospects.projection: A second-wave evaluation for Pewter, where Unown has made thirteen of nineteen field-goal attempts and competition could be useful if the direct kicking comparison supports it.

prospects.name: Grubbin
prospects.analysis: Coumarine Coastal University's Grubbin has the same age and vertical as North Kalos's prospect, with a 57–85 band and level thirteen. The 5.06 forty and six bench repetitions trail his counterpart; the 6.89 cone edges him. I place him seventh because the total visible case is slightly less persuasive, then immediately note how easily an actual kicking session could reverse those two names. This is exactly the part of a board where a confident scout should stop mistaking a numbered list for certainty.
prospects.concern: No recorded college kick separates him from the Grubbin above. Similarity in the available measurements is a reason to investigate, not to merge their identities.
prospects.projection: Evaluate beside North Kalos's Grubbin rather than after him as an afterthought. Canalave's thirteen-for-nineteen field-goal line supplies a reasonable team for that comparison.

prospects.name: Koffing
prospects.analysis: Ole Fallarbor's Koffing is my familiar Hoenn temptation, and I am keeping him eighth anyway. At twenty-three and level twenty-four, he enters at the highest visible level in the group, shared with Charjabug. The 57–85 band matches Coumarine's Grubbin; the workout reads 5.12, nine bench repetitions, thirty-two inches and 6.99. There is no dramatic movement advantage to sell. There is an established development marker worth comparing against younger, less advanced prospects. I would like that comparison to happen with a football on a tee.
prospects.concern: The older age and advanced level do not tell us how much useful improvement remains. No growth promise is supported here.
prospects.projection: Mauville should evaluate the local-region option without allowing familiarity to decide it. He belongs in the same working session as Charjabug, not in a separate sentimental category.

prospects.name: Yamask
prospects.analysis: Po State's Yamask has a 54–82 band at twenty-two and level ten. The 5.12 forty, nine bench repetitions, thirty-two-inch vertical and 7.05 cone create a conventional lower-middle workout profile. I am putting him ninth because the visible range trails the central cluster, not because his movement disqualifies him from a position built around a different task. A club conducting a genuine specialist search should still collect the missing kicking evidence. There is no prize for rejecting a workable leg because somebody else ran a tidier shuttle.
prospects.concern: The current evidence does not identify either a standout athletic advantage or a superior scouting band.
prospects.projection: A later comparison for a club seeking a second kicking option; the actual roster fit still has to justify the place.

prospects.name: Meditite
prospects.analysis: Viridian State's Meditite is twenty-one and level fifteen, with a 47–75 band. The 4.93 forty and 6.75 cone are better movement numbers than those of several players above him. That is why I want the direct evaluation before dismissing him, and why I still will not move him past prospects with much stronger visible bands merely to reward the stopwatch. Thirty-four inches in the vertical and nine bench repetitions complete a profile that is athletic enough to ask a second question.
prospects.concern: The lower scouting interval is a real caution. Youth is not evidence of a guaranteed improvement path.
prospects.projection: A developmental competition candidate after the leading group. Teams with dependable incumbents should compare his future role against other roster needs before spending a pick.

prospects.name: Skitty
prospects.analysis: University of Cortondo's Skitty is the youngest tier of this class at twenty-one, with level thirteen and a 44–72 interval. A 4.99 forty, thirty-five-inch jump and 6.85 cone keep the movement respectable. Eight bench repetitions add little separation. I prefer the age and slightly stronger band floor to the final two entries, but the kicking question remains almost entirely open. The sensible response is a targeted workout, not a promise that an attractive young athlete will eventually solve a specialist job.
prospects.concern: Neither the low-end band nor the absence of direct kicking measurements supports an immediate-starter claim.
prospects.projection: A later developmental evaluation for a team that can afford patience; I would not ask an offense already struggling to score to assume he is ready.

prospects.name: Combee
prospects.analysis: Dewford University's Combee gives me another Hoenn athlete to admire: 4.89 in the forty, thirty-eight inches vertically and 6.70 through the cones. Those are better movement marks than his 44–72 band might lead a casual reader to expect. He is twenty-three and level six, so I rank him twelfth rather than inventing a long development runway from the workout alone. Brawly's current Numel has made ten of twelve field goals. The college name is pleasant; it does not create a vacancy on the Breakers.
prospects.concern: The athletic display does not resolve placement, distance or the meaning of the low scouting interval. The oldest age tier merits care in developmental projections.
prospects.projection: A specialist-session invitation before a draft commitment. Dewford should evaluate on merit while treating its productive incumbent as a real comparison.

prospects.name: Munna
prospects.analysis: University of Violet's Munna closes the list at twenty-three and level sixteen. His 43–71 band is the lowest here, and the 5.13 forty, five bench repetitions and 7.26 cone do not supply an athletic reason to override it. The twenty-nine-inch vertical is tied at the bottom. I am comfortable ranking this visible case thirteenth. I am less comfortable telling a reader that it proves he cannot kick, because none of those measurements records an attempt through the uprights.
prospects.concern: Every broad indicator leaves work to do, and direct specialist evidence is still absent. This is the weakest current case, not a hidden discovery I can honestly sell.
prospects.projection: A late evaluation only if the actual kicking session changes the discussion. Do not spend ahead of the stronger visible candidates on a story the evidence has not told.

art.alt: Accumula State prospect Maractus works through a kick during a practice drill.

articles.title: Count the next down
articles.dek: Saffron made eight sacks decide possessions. Blackthorn scored through four. The difference should change how we talk about protection.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Blayz Matthews sacked Hatterene on the first offensive play at Mt. Silver. Six yards gone. Second-and-sixteen. That is the moment when a defense has earned an advantage and still has work to do. Hatterene threw short left to Tinkaton for thirty-one yards on the next snap. The opening drive ended in a Blackthorn touchdown. If your account of that possession stops at the sack, you have stopped watching precisely when the important question begins.

I want the league's contenders judged by what pressure makes happen next. A sack can ruin a drive, shorten the available decisions or merely interrupt an offense that still knows where to go. Week 12 supplied all three possibilities. Saffron's eight-sack demolition of Cinnabar was the strongest example of pressure becoming control. Mt. Silver's first defeat was the warning against assuming the conversion happens automatically.

Matthews had three sacks. The Reds had four altogether. Blackthorn still scored on its first six possessions and won 30–22. That does not make Matthews's work worthless, and it does not mean Clair should be content to watch her quarterback lose twenty-five yards to sacks. It means the defenders' successful rushes and the offense's successful responses belong in the same analysis. Counting only the part that flatters your preferred argument is how a useful number becomes a very bad explanation.

Watch Tinkaton's second rescue. Matthews had again put Hatterene backward, this time by seven yards. An incompletion left third-and-seventeen. Hatterene threw deep left to Tinkaton for twenty-four. Cacturne eventually made a field goal. The defense had obtained a long-yardage situation and still allowed the receiver to gain more than the required distance. That is a coverage and completion problem after a pass-rush success. The first accomplishment cannot be used as an alibi for the second failure.

Blackthorn's passing answers also changed shape. The initial recovery went short left. The next important conversion went deep left. On the drive before halftime, Hatterene followed another Matthews sack with a twenty-one-yard completion deep right to Seadra. The Dragons were not asking one desperate throw in one direction to repair everything. They kept finding a receiving answer that fit the next opportunity. Their 28 completions in 38 attempts tell the broader story; those individual responses tell us how it survived the pressure.

I wanted to make the next play easier for everybody. Hatterene put the ball where I could help. Getting the yards after a sack doesn't mean the last play didn't matter. It means we still had work we could do.
body.speaker: Tinkaton

body.text: Now turn to Cinnabar. After a twenty-five-yard completion opened the second half, Demedicus Ware sacked Gholdengo for five yards, then seven. Third-and-twenty-three followed. Gholdengo ran for four, and the Blaze punted. Here the pressure did not just create a photograph of a defender reaching the quarterback. It removed the offense's promising position and made the remaining down insufficient to recover it. That is the full sequence Trent Scarboro can carry into the next defensive meeting.

Ware's seventh sack might be the more revealing one. A Tatsugiri interception had given Cinnabar first-and-six at the beginning of the fourth quarter. This was the offense's chance to benefit from its defense. An incompletion and a one-yard run left third-and-four. Ware pushed Gholdengo backward seven yards, and the Blaze settled for a field goal. Saffron had made a short field longer at the moment when Cinnabar needed it to become a touchdown.

There is a real difference between those two defensive performances. Cinnabar finished one-of-nine on third down and scored three points. Blackthorn went five-of-ten and scored thirty. The Dragons did not throw an interception or lose a fumble; the Blaze did not either. This comparison is not being distorted by one side repeatedly donating short-field possessions. It is about what the offenses could still accomplish after the rush had won a snap.

I also want some precision about the word protection. The recorded plays show sacks, pass directions, completions and results. They do not tell us that every sack belongs to one lineman, or that a particular unrecorded adjustment created the answer. I won't invent a missed assignment to make the argument sound more technical. What we can see is enough: Hatterene repeatedly had productive passing responses on the following downs. Gholdengo increasingly did not.

That gives the coaches different problems. Connor McLarren needs the rush and the defense behind it to finish the same possession. Four sacks are not evidence that his unit had Blackthorn under control when the first six drives all produced points. Blaine needs a more usable offensive response when the pocket fails, because Cinnabar's seven rushing attempts yielded eight yards and could not relieve the passing burden. Those are separate coaching assignments. Neither is solved by demanding that everybody simply want it more.
We made negative plays and still let them keep drives alive. That is the part we have to correct. Getting the quarterback down helps only if we finish the work on the downs after it.
body.speaker: Connor McLarren

body.text: Eterna offered a third useful version at the end of its 14–6 win over Sunyshore. The Thorns did not record their first sack until the fourth quarter. Charjabug's seven-yard stop on third-and-seven preceded a missed fifty-three-yard field goal. On the final Starseekers possession, Rampardos and Klawf produced consecutive sacks on third and fourth down. Three sacks, all in the last quarter, each attached to an immediate ending that favored Eterna. Timing and consequence supplied the meaning.

The Thorns had also stopped a fourth-down pass with Parasect's breakup before those final sacks. That matters because defensive control does not require the same finish every time. Sometimes the quarterback goes down. Sometimes the receiver never gets the ball. The common achievement is that the offense runs out of downs before it earns what it needs. I want that connection in the evaluation, alongside the individual player who made the final play.

My position is simple: praise the rush, then keep watching. Saffron earned the right to celebrate eight sacks because its pressure repeatedly left Cinnabar without a useful next answer. Blackthorn earned the right to celebrate 358 passing yards because its passing game survived four sacks and kept finishing drives. Mt. Silver is still a contender. It is also a contender that now has direct evidence of where a successful rush stopped being a successful possession. Fix that part. The sack total already knows how to look impressive.

articles.title: Give the next quarterback a smaller job
articles.dek: Lavender’s comeback showed how many players can carry a possession. That is the lesson to keep while Mr. Clanky is out.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Frosmoth completed nine passes at Cianwood. One won Lavender the chance to take the lead, another rescued fourth-and-thirteen, and several others kept the final drive from becoming a moving description of disappointment. It is tempting to turn those completions into a new quarterback story immediately. I would prefer to begin with all the people who made it possible for nine to be enough.

Mr. Clanky is out two weeks. That is the news Travis Scarboro must prepare around after the 18–17 victory. Frosmoth supplied 113 passing yards and the late touchdown to Luvdisc, while Zorua's four earlier attempts produced no completions and an interception. The available evidence gives Frosmoth a substantial claim to consideration for the next assignment. It does not oblige Lavender to ask him to become the whole offense by next week.

My position is that the Wails should make the replacement quarterback's job more manageable by making everybody else's job more explicit. The winning possession already offered a useful example. Luvdisc made catches. Kujira supplied the fourth-down conversion. Machoke, Samurott and Hobbes moved the ball afterward. Frosmoth connected those contributions. He did not conjure ninety-six yards without assistance, and nobody should turn a celebration into that expectation.
I want to get back to it. There were throws I could have made sooner and chances I want again. The guys kept giving me another place to go with the ball. I need to make that easier for them, too.
body.speaker: Frosmoth

body.text: That eagerness is useful. So is a little perspective from the player whose absence created the next problem. Clanky had thrown for 223 yards in the previous week's win over Veilstone. His latest game produced one completion for one yard before the offense moved through other passers. A new injury and a tiny passing line are not a referendum on everything he contributed before them. The Wails can prepare for his absence without pretending that a late comeback has settled the longer quarterback question forever.
They finished the job. I liked that they kept finding each other. That's what I want us to keep.
body.speaker: Mr. Clanky

body.text: I would keep that last sentence near the preparation notes. Lavender's recent good work has come when the offense found more than one contributor. Diggersby ran for 101 yards in the 31–14 win over Veilstone. Hobbes gained 118 at Cianwood, while Frosmoth found a different receiving connection late. These are examples of an offense discovering useful help, not proof that the same player must carry the same number of touches every week. The stable principle can be shared work even when the names doing it change.

There is a practical reason to be modest about the winning passing line. Frosmoth was sacked four times. Lavender converted only two of ten third downs. Before the final touchdown drive, the second half had produced a field goal and a succession of punts. The comeback was earned, but it did not erase the difficult possessions that made a ninety-six-yard finish necessary. A plan built only from the last drive would remember the exhilaration and forget why there was so much ground left to cover.

Scarboro should want more completions that prevent fourth-and-thirteen from becoming part of the regular job description. On the winning drive, Frosmoth hit Luvdisc for nineteen yards and fifteen before the later trouble. Those catches gave the possession a beginning. Samurott's seven-yard catch and Machoke's ten-yard catch helped give it an ending. Asking a quarterback to keep locating such useful contributions is more reasonable than asking him to reproduce Kujira's dramatic rescue on demand.

The running work should receive the same respect. Hobbes gained ten up the middle and fourteen to the left late in the drive. His first long run had gone fifty-six yards earlier in the game, but those later gains were important in a different way: they moved a tired, urgent possession closer to a finish without requiring another completed throw. Machoke's two-point run then decided the score. Lavender's best passing moment ended with the ball in a runner's hands.

We have to help the person taking the snap. That means catching the available ball, making the run useful and keeping a bad play from becoming a bad series. The finish gave us something to build on. It didn't finish the preparation for us.
body.speaker: Travis Scarboro

body.text: People Eater remains out five weeks. Beedrill's injury counter has reached zero, which is encouraging availability news without establishing what his next workload will be. Those details should make the offensive conversation more careful, not more dramatic. The Wails do not have to invent a new identity for every missing receiver. They do need a clear sense of which available players have already shown they can catch a useful pass and help the next passer get through a possession.

Luvdisc's five catches for sixty-nine yards are worth remembering in that discussion. Kujira's one catch mattered enormously, but it was still one catch. The sensible response is to appreciate both kinds of contribution without turning either into a demand for a larger performance the following week. A target can be valuable because he stays available repeatedly; another can be valuable because he makes the one difficult catch that arrives. The quarterback needs ways to recognize and use both.

The defense also has a place in the next quarterback's working conditions. Cianwood scored seventeen points before halftime and none afterward. That kept Lavender close while its offense was changing passers and losing possessions. Scarboro cannot promise another second-half shutout against Mahogany, but he can fairly ask that the defense remain part of the solution. A replacement passer should not inherit the quiet assumption that every difficulty elsewhere must now be repaired through his arm.

At 6–5, the Wails have moved into sixth in the current Kanto–Johto seeding order. The position matters. It also makes grand declarations especially unhelpful. There are still games to win and availability questions to manage, beginning with Mahogany's visit. Lavender does not need to choose between enjoying the comeback and being honest about the work ahead. Those are compatible activities, even if one produces a much nicer interview than the other.

I like the way this team won because it did not wait for the afternoon to become tidy. The passer changed. The useful runner changed from the previous week. The decisive receiver caught one ball, and the winning points came from a two-yard run. Give Frosmoth credit for his part. Give the next quarterback enough help that his part remains possible. The most encouraging thing about Lavender's finish was how many players could claim a necessary sentence in it.

art.alt: Lavender’s Frosmoth faces the light at the end of a stadium tunnel.

articles.title: Candice, keep the ordinary answers
articles.dek: Snowpoint’s third victory supplied something more useful than a flattering score: an offense that could keep the ball without waiting for a gift.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Snowpoint completed twenty-four passes, ran for 101 yards and won 24–6. There. A functioning offensive afternoon, announced without a trumpet, a parade or a claim that 3–8 is secretly an excellent record. I would like Candice to keep the film, underline the useful parts and resist anyone who suggests the entire season has suddenly been redeemed. One good game is enough to examine. It does not need to be promoted into a fairy tale before lunch.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: competence becomes more valuable when a losing team can explain where it came from. Snowpoint did not receive a collection of turnovers and congratulate itself for finding the end zone nearby. The Blizzard's touchdown drives covered ninety-one, seventy-two and eighty yards. Those are long trips. They required the offense to perform several ordinary jobs in succession. That is the part I want retained after the pleasant score stops being new.

Drampa completed twenty-four of thirty-one for 220 yards and a touchdown, with no interceptions. Oinkologne ran fifteen times for seventy-five yards. Abomasnow caught eight passes for eighty-eight yards and a score. These totals do not demand that we imagine a superstar transformation. They describe a quarterback finding receivers, a runner supplying usable gains and a team converting seven of ten third downs. I am aware that this sounds basic. Snowpoint has earned the right to be praised for doing the basics together.

Start with the opening touchdown drive, which began at the Blizzard nine. Oinkologne lost a yard, and Drampa found Abomasnow deep right for twenty-four. Later, third-and-ten arrived after a run for no gain and an incompletion. Drampa threw short left to Gastrodon for sixteen. That completion is more useful to the next week's preparation than a general instruction to be confident. It shows a difficult down becoming a first down through an available receiver.

The drive kept moving through different contributors. Oinkologne gained nine up the middle. Audino caught two. Hawlucha caught twenty-four deep left. Castform caught twelve short right and then ran the final five yards to the left for the touchdown. Eleven offensive plays carried Snowpoint ninety-one yards. No single player had to pretend he could do every job. That is an excellent arrangement for a team that has spent too much of its season asking a modest offense to solve enormous problems.
The receivers kept giving me somewhere to put the ball. The runs helped us stay in the drive, too. I don't think it belongs to one person. We kept doing enough on the next play.
body.speaker: Drampa

body.text: Modest. Accurate. Almost suspiciously reasonable for a quarterback whose team has just won by eighteen. I will supply the volume he has declined to provide: KEEP DOING ENOUGH. Not occasionally. Not only when the first play works. The next possession included another third-and-nine, and Drampa again found Gastrodon short left, this time for fourteen yards. A useful answer had appeared twice. Candice should be more interested in that repetition than in finding a glamorous description for the whole afternoon.

Anorith helped keep that second touchdown drive alive with seven yards up the middle on third-and-four. Spidops caught consecutive six-yard passes. Oinkologne supplied another seven-yard run and a short reception. Drampa finished from a yard out with 2:00 left in the second quarter. Seventy-two yards, fourteen offensive plays, another touchdown. Snowpoint had followed a long opening drive with another one, which is how evidence begins to become an argument rather than a happy accident.

I am not suggesting every third down was easy or that the Blizzard have discovered a permanent guarantee. The offense still punted three times. Drampa was sacked twice late. The game did not end with Snowpoint marching endlessly down the field. That is precisely why the useful sequences deserve to be identified. A coach needs the parts that can be worked on again, not a vague command to repeat the final score.

The eighty-yard touchdown drive after halftime might be the best teaching material. Drampa found Abomasnow for fourteen over the middle on second-and-eleven, then ten to the right on second-and-nine. Anorith later converted third-and-three with a four-yard run. When third-and-eight arrived near the end of the drive, Drampa went back to Abomasnow over the middle for nine. The next throw went short left to the same receiver for an eleven-yard touchdown.

That was a receiver doing more than furnishing a highlight. Abomasnow helped repair two longer second downs, converted a third down and finished the drive. The passing game had a dependable destination without becoming a one-player operation. Oinkologne, Anorith and Audino had also contributed along the way. Fourteen plays consumed 4:03 and produced a 24–0 lead. A team can make a great deal of useful trouble by simply refusing to give the ball away cheaply.
I was glad the ball came my way when we needed it. There were good throws and a lot of work before those catches. I'd rather we keep that going than make too much of my part.
body.speaker: Abomasnow

body.text: Fine, Abomasnow. I will make a controlled amount of your part. Eight catches. Eighty-eight yards. One touchdown. Enough to matter, not enough to excuse the rest of the offense from continuing to help. That is the standard I want for Snowpoint: important players receiving credit without the team immediately deciding that they must provide every future answer alone.

The defense earned its share. The Blizzard allowed no touchdown, recorded five pass breakups and held the opposition to three conversions in nine third-down attempts. Finizen's seven-yard sack late in the third quarter helped turn a promising drive into a field-goal possession. Porygon2 had earlier stopped a fourth-and-one run for no gain, giving the offense a chance to add three points before halftime. The offense's long drives and the defense's finishing plays made sense together.

There is now a costly personnel problem. Jumpluff is listed out eleven weeks after a new injury. That is a serious absence at cornerback, and the win does not make it smaller. Medicham has a minor injury entry with zero weeks remaining. Those are different pieces of availability information. Candice needs to manage the missing coverage work while preserving the offense's progress; declaring that momentum will cover the vacancy would be a charming way to avoid an actual responsibility.

We finished drives because several players kept contributing. That has to stay part of what we do next. The injury changes some of the work ahead, but it doesn't change the standard we need from the whole team.
body.speaker: Candice

body.text: The Blizzard are still 3–8, with 150 points scored and 168 allowed. They are also winless in four road games and travel to Oreburgh next. That is a concrete next test for the useful habits shown here. I am not handing out a forecasted resurrection. I want the quarterback to keep finding the available catch, the runners to keep making the following down manageable and the defense to give those possessions a chance to matter.

Snowpoint has not earned a grand proclamation. It has earned a much more practical demand. Candice, keep the ordinary answers: the third-down throw to Gastrodon, the run that converts, the patient return to Abomasnow, the possession that survives a bad first play. Three touchdown drives covered 243 yards. None began as a gift. That is football you can ask your team to build again. Do that before anyone starts naming the comeback tour.

articles.title: The waiting room is full: Week 12 injury report
articles.dek: Sixteen new absences, ten cleared recovery counters, and a changing cast for the playoff push. Ninjaskamara, Mr. Clanky and My Way, Son headline the league-wide report.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: The recovery room has become one of the league's busiest meeting places. Week 12 produced sixteen new injuries carrying a reported absence, and the list reaches directly into the playoff race: Mossdeep's leading rusher, Lavender's quarterback, Rustboro's rushing group and Vermilion's defensive depth. Winning the afternoon has not guaranteed an uncomplicated week of preparation.

Across the league, fifty-three players now carry a positive recovery counter. Ten players who had time remaining in the previous report have reached zero or had that designation cleared. Those are different kinds of movement. A counter changing from four weeks to three is continuing recovery; it is not another injury. A counter reaching zero also does not, by itself, establish a return to the lineup.

This report reflects confirmed information after Week 12 and before Week 13. Durations below are the reported recovery counts, not guaranteed dates for the next appearance. The game records identify injuries but do not establish when during a game each occurred. We can describe who produced in the recorded game; we cannot attach an injury to a particular collision unless the record supports it.
Mossdeep's clinch comes with a backfield problem

Ninjaskamara has a four-week injury entry after the 35–7 win at Rustboro. The Ninjask still leads the league with 1,138 rushing yards, so this is a meaningful change to an offense that has been able to ask different players to finish drives. He carried three times for sixteen yards in Week 12. His absence now stretches beyond the immediate trip to Fortree on the reported counter.

Poury Holt supplied an actual answer during the game: sixteen carries for eighty-two yards, including the eight-yard third-down conversion that kept the first touchdown drive of the second half alive. That production gives Michael Dorrill something concrete to build on. It does not make the lost workload disappear, and a strong rushing performance is not a guarantee of the next week's final deployment.

Richard Furman is also out for a reported five weeks. Listed as a cornerback, the Meowth nevertheless carried four times for thirty yards at Rustboro. That is why the position label alone does not describe everything Mossdeep loses. Marshall Flock's existing absence is now three weeks, down from four. The Eclipse have secured Hoenn East; getting there has not made their available personnel a fixed quantity.
Lavender must prepare beyond the rescue

Mr. Clanky's two-week entry changes the conversation around Lavender's 18–17 escape at Cianwood. The Iron Bundle completed one of four passes for one yard. Frosmoth supplied nine completions on twenty attempts for 113 yards and the late touchdown to Luvdisc, while Zorua also threw four passes and an interception. The combined passing line should not be mistaken for one replacement's afternoon.

Frosmoth has the most substantial recent passing evidence among those alternatives. His twenty-two-yard fourth-down completion to Kujira on the winning drive is a reason to take that evidence seriously. Four sacks are a reason to give the protection equal attention. With Mahogany visiting next, Travis Scarboro needs a plan that accounts for both, rather than asking one comeback to settle the entire quarterback discussion.

People Eater remains out for five weeks, down from six. Beedrill's previous one-week designation has reached zero. That change adds an availability question worth following, but the cleared counter does not establish a restored receiving role. Lavender's immediate concern is distributing a real workload among the players who can take it.
The other backfields have changed too

Rustboro's My Way, Son carries a six-week entry after two rushing attempts for five yards against Mossdeep. Philly ran twelve times for sixty-one yards, and Watchog added forty-five on nine carries. Those are recorded alternatives for the Stone's upcoming meeting with Mauville. Philly also has a new minor entry with no remaining absence; the report gives no basis for turning that into a multiweek diagnosis.

Mauville has its own severe disruption: Unfezant's new recovery count is thirteen weeks. Sootopolis lists Arbok at seventeen weeks, another new injury whose duration reaches well beyond the remaining regular-season schedule. Those counters warrant planning for substantial absences. They do not justify inventing a specific medical condition or a firm postseason return date.

Blackthorn beat Mt. Silver while Furret's game produced a two-week entry. The Dragons visit Violet next; Violet has new two-week absences for both Barbaracle and Snorlax. Olivine, traveling to Mt. Silver, adds Delcatty for three weeks while several earlier absences continue. None of these clubs gets to treat next week's matchup as an exact replay of the personnel available in the last one.
Vermilion's win carries a defensive bill

The Volts won 7–6 at Viridian and now face Saffron with two substantial new defensive absences: Gabite, a defensive end, is listed at seven weeks, and cornerback Drakloak at fifteen. Tentacruel's previous one-week designation has reached zero, but one cleared cornerback entry cannot be treated as proof that every coverage problem is solved. Saffron just produced 324 passing yards and three passing touchdowns at Cinnabar.

The Psi Corps receive two encouraging changes of their own. NeMarcus Tare and Verrick Brooks have both reached zero after carrying one week in the prior report. Neither should be credited with playing in the Cinnabar game merely because the current counter has cleared. Demedicus Ware's eight recorded sacks are already in the book; decisions about how the available linebackers share the next game remain ahead.

Snowpoint's 24–6 win brings an eleven-week injury for cornerback Jumpluff. The Blizzard can enjoy a much cleaner offensive afternoon and still have a significant defensive absence to manage before visiting Oreburgh. Elsewhere, Cerulean's Raticate and Oreburgh's Huntail each carry new two-week entries, while Celadon's Anorith is listed for five.

articles.title: The road team meets the perfect home record: Dewford at Petalburg
articles.dek: Four straight Dewford wins meet three straight for Petalburg, with the Hoenn West gap at one game. After both teams leaned on punt-return touchdowns, Tessa Wren asks whose ordinary offense can decide the rematch.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Petalburg and Dewford reached this meeting with winning streaks, productive runners and an unusually helpful contribution from the punt-return unit. Flygon went eighty yards for a Pride touchdown. Meowscarada went seventy-five for the Breakers. Both plays belong in the explanation of last week's victories. Neither belongs in the advance budget for the next one. My question for the Game of the Week is what happens when two good teams have to pay for more of their points through ordinary offensive possessions.

Petalburg is 8–3, has won three straight and remains unbeaten in five home games. Dewford is 7–4, has won four straight and has taken four of five road games. These are the two best records in Hoenn West, separated by one game. A Breakers win leaves both teams 8–4; a Pride win makes them 9–3 and 7–5. That is a substantial swing with five regular-season games left afterward. The rematch also matters because Norman's team won the opening meeting 19–12 at Dewford.

My forecast is Petalburg, 23–20. I trust Oinkologne's involvement and the Pride's season-long resistance to the run a little more than I trust Dewford to repeat a low-volume passing victory without another return touchdown. It is a small edge. The Breakers have the pressure and receiving threat to overturn it, and Petalburg's seven completions against Sootopolis are a perfectly reasonable starting point for an objection. A 5–0 home record does not complete the next pass.
Two wins, two short routes to the end zone

The Pride beat Sootopolis 21–18 despite being outgained 338–228. At 4:26 of the second quarter, Flygon returned a punt eighty yards for the touchdown that put Petalburg ahead. The offense supplied the other two touchdowns, including a thirteen-play, seventy-three-yard drive finished by Iron Valiant's four-yard throw to Venomoth. That matters: the Pride did demonstrate they could assemble a full possession. They also received seven points without asking their passer to assemble anything.

Dewford's 22–16 win over Lavaridge had a similar imbalance. The Inferno gained 283 yards to the Breakers' 189. With 1:23 left in the third quarter, Meowscarada returned a punt seventy-five yards for a touchdown. The Breakers also intercepted Delphox twice and did not lose a turnover. Those are valuable ways to help an offense. The caution is that Frosmoth threw only ten passes, and Dewford converted two of seven third downs. Twenty-two points did not represent twenty-two points of dependable drive construction.

The right conclusion is not that either result was undeserved. Returns and takeaways count, and both clubs made the plays that won. The next question is whether they can protect themselves if the extra help does not recur. Punt coverage deserves particular attention after those two touchdowns. A return that merely gives the offense a short field could matter almost as much in a game where neither side has regularly needed a huge passing total to stay competitive.
Oinkologne sets Petalburg's terms

Oinkologne has 736 rushing yards on 152 carries this season, about 4.8 per attempt. He gained seventy-three on fourteen against Sootopolis. Petalburg has 1,106 team rushing yards and has allowed 773, while Dewford has gained 1,228 and allowed 984. Those totals cover eleven games for each club. They suggest the Pride are better positioned to limit the opponent's ordinary ground gains, although they do not guarantee which runner wins this particular afternoon. Dewford's front must make the hosts earn more difficult passing downs.

The most persuasive Petalburg sequence came at the end of the Sootopolis game. The Pride took possession with 4:01 remaining and a three-point lead. After a run for no gain and a sack, Iron Valiant faced third-and-sixteen. His short-right pass to Seviper gained twenty-two. Oinkologne then supplied consecutive seven-yard runs, right and up the middle, before Whiscash and the quarterback helped close out the game. Sootopolis never got another possession. That is a useful demonstration of how an imperfect passing day can still finish with the necessary throw.

It is also a sequence Dewford should be determined not to repeat. The Breakers have to finish the possession when the distance favors them. Watchog recorded two sacks against Lavaridge, with Ambipom adding another. Pressure that creates third-and-long only completes half the assignment; Seviper's conversion shows what can happen to the other half. Norman should not ask Iron Valiant to live in that situation. He should use Oinkologne's steady involvement to keep it an occasional rescue rather than the operating plan.

Iron Valiant has seventeen passing touchdowns against six interceptions this season, so the last seven-for-twenty-one line is not the only evidence available. Yet Petalburg's most recent receiving distribution warrants care: Seviper caught three of ten targets, and Venomoth one of five, the touchdown. Golbat's two catches produced fifty-one yards. I want more successful ordinary throws before assuming the Pride can simply pass their way out of a stalled ground game. Dewford can make a modest scoring target sufficient if it keeps those completions scarce.
Dewford has a useful answer beyond waiting

The Breakers' best offensive possession against Lavaridge lasted four plays and covered fifty-two yards. Frosmoth found Swellow deep right for twenty-two, then Machoke short left for fourteen. Unfezant ran left for nine and up the middle for the final seven-yard touchdown. That sequence gives Brawly a concrete model for this matchup: a productive throw outside, another useful receiving option, and a runner finishing while the defense still has several things to consider. It was compact offense, not an argument for avoiding offense.

Swellow caught all three of his targets for seventy-two yards in that game. Across the season he has 291 receiving yards in nine appearances. He is a meaningful threat, but Dewford cannot assume three catches will again supply most of its passing production. Infernape has 288 season receiving yards and Watchog 236. Those alternative contributors matter if Petalburg keeps Swellow from turning a small target count into the whole aerial answer. The roles shown by their production are more useful here than an assumption about one receiver carrying every drive.

Frosmoth has seventeen touchdown passes and eleven interceptions through eleven games. The clean latest performance is encouraging; the longer turnover record is the reason I want a controlled passing assignment. Petalburg sacked Drampa four times, including one and a half for Girafarig. Vileplume intercepted Drampa, and Toedscruel recovered a fumble. If Dewford falls behind and has to keep asking for difficult throws, the Pride have recent evidence of how they can make those possessions end. A balanced start is therefore a practical need, not a stylistic preference.

Unfezant's season rushing total is 557 yards on 131 carries. Against Lavaridge he gained fifty-seven and scored once, while Gumshoos supplied thirty yards and the other rushing touchdown. Brawly has more than one recent contributor to use. The challenge is making those ordinary gains last against Petalburg's stronger season rushing resistance. A few successful early possessions would keep Frosmoth from having to chase the score and make the Pride's own passing limitations much more relevant to the result.
The margin includes health, kicks and the next month

Neither club has a current injury absence with remaining weeks. Dewford's Gliscor received a minor entry against Lavaridge and has no remaining absence reported; that is different from inventing a lingering doubtful designation. Petalburg has no current injury entry. Compared with several contenders managing newly injured quarterbacks or runners, these coaches can prepare around their established contributors. That makes the execution question sharper. There is no confirmed absence here that explains away a failure to finish a block, cover a punt or secure a routine throw.

Special teams extend beyond the two return touchdowns. Petalburg's Sunflora has made all nine season field-goal attempts and twenty-four of twenty-six extra points. Dewford's Numel is ten-for-twelve on field goals and nineteen-for-twenty-two on extra points, but made only one of three extra points against Lavaridge. His twenty-two-yard field goal with 1:55 left still pushed that lead to six. In a forecast separated by a field goal, those small scoring decisions deserve attention without assuming either kicker will repeat last week's exact afternoon.

The schedule gives the division stakes another edge. Petalburg follows this game with trips to unbeaten Mossdeep and improving Pastoria, then hosts Eterna. Dewford goes to Sootopolis and Hearthome before hosting Oreburgh. Both finish with Mauville and Rustboro in the last two weeks, in different orders. These are opportunities and obstacles, not automatic wins. A two-game gap would give the Pride useful room before a demanding stretch; a level record would give the Breakers a very different view of the same month.

For Dewford, the winning route is a clean Frosmoth game, enough early rushing to keep the offense balanced, and pressure that actually ends Petalburg possessions. For the Pride, it is Oinkologne keeping the next throw manageable, coverage that makes the Breakers use more than Swellow, and another finish with the ball securely in their hands. I expect Petalburg to find one extra sustained possession, even if the return units stay out of the end zone. Pride 23, Breakers 20.

articles.title: Mossdeep is in. Mt. Silver has two routes to follow.
articles.dek: The Eclipse have secured Hoenn East. Ellis Quill maps every Week 13 clinching route, the ties that matter and the matchups reshaping both playoff fields.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Mossdeep can put one argument away. The Eclipse are Hoenn East champions, and their playoff place is secured. Their 35–7 victory at Rustboro supplied the eleventh win; defeats for Sootopolis and Lavaridge removed the last mathematical obstacle. Michael Dorrill’s club has been playing like a postseason team for months. Now the standings have stopped leaving room for an objection.

That is the only qualification already settled. Mt. Silver’s 30–22 loss to Blackthorn ended the Reds’ unbeaten run and left their invitation unsigned. Week 13 offers a much simpler division-clinching assignment: beat visiting Olivine. There is also a precise three-game route if the Reds tie. Those are the complete new clinching possibilities this week under the league’s published playoff rules. No other club can secure a new berth or division title, and neither conference’s first-round bye can be clinched.
Mossdeep’s banner is earned; the rest is still work

At 11–0, Mossdeep already has more wins than any Hoenn East rival can finish with. Sootopolis and Lavaridge are 4–7 with six games remaining, giving each a ceiling of ten victories. Fortree is 3–8 and can reach nine. No tiebreak is needed. The Eclipse have won the division outright even in the worst remaining sequence of results.

body.title: Confirmed through Week 12: Mossdeep wins Hoenn East
body.description: Season 1, Week 12 confirmed outcome. The three completed results below satisfied the division route.

steps.label: AND Sootopolis loses
steps.text: Surge lose 21–18 at Petalburg; maximum finish is ten wins.

steps.label: AND Lavaridge loses
steps.text: Inferno lose 22–16 at Dewford; maximum finish is ten wins.

steps.label: Division clinched
steps.text: Mossdeep secures Hoenn East and a playoff berth. The first seed remains open.

body.text: The next opponent is Fortree, followed by Petalburg at home, Canalave away and Sunyshore at home. That three-game stretch from Weeks 14 through 16 crosses three current division leaders. Sootopolis at home and Lavaridge away complete the schedule. A secured division allows the Eclipse to look up the bracket; it does not make those appointments ceremonial.

Sunyshore’s 14–6 loss at Eterna has widened the distance at the top. The Starseekers are 8–3, three wins behind Mossdeep, with a Week 16 trip to the Eclipse still available as a direct opportunity. They visit Hearthome next, then host Canalave and Rustboro. My first-seed choice remains Mossdeep. But even an Eclipse win this week leaves a possible finish in which Sunyshore wins its final five games and ends above a Mossdeep side that loses out. Only the first seed rests in the opening round, and that rest has not been reserved.
Mt. Silver route one: beat Olivine

A Reds victory produces an 11–1 record and clinches Johto West. Olivine would fall to 6–6, leaving the Ironclads able to reach eleven wins only by sweeping their final five games. Mt. Silver already beat Olivine 13–9 in Week 1. A second victory would complete the head-to-head sweep and settle that possible eleven-win tie in the Reds’ favor. Azalea can finish with no more than ten wins; Cianwood can reach nine.

body.title: Week 13 route A: Mt. Silver clinches the division
body.description: Season 1, Week 13 conditional route. This route needs no help from another game.

steps.label: Mt. Silver wins
steps.text: Reds beat Olivine and improve to 11–1.

steps.label: Head-to-head sweep secured
steps.text: Olivine can finish with eleven wins at most; Mt. Silver would own both meetings.

steps.label: Division clinched
steps.text: Johto West and a playoff berth belong to Mt. Silver. The first seed remains open.

body.text: This is an unusually direct reward for recovering from a defeat. Blackthorn has made the conference race tighter, but the Reds do not need to watch Saffron or calculate a margin of victory to claim their own division. They need one more win over the nearest divisional pursuer. The first meeting was decided by four points, which is a useful antidote to treating the requirement as a formality.
Mt. Silver route two: a tie and two specific favors

If Mt. Silver ties Olivine, it can secure a playoff berth only if Blackthorn beats Violet AND Mahogany beats Lavender. Both supporting results must be outright wins. A tie in either supporting game is insufficient. This combination guarantees entry to the postseason while leaving Johto West open; Olivine could still finish above the Reds.

body.title: Week 13 route B: Mt. Silver secures a berth
body.description: Season 1, Week 13 conditional route. ALL three results are required; this is an alternative to route A.

steps.label: Mt. Silver ties
steps.text: Reds and Olivine finish level; Mt. Silver becomes 10–1–1.

steps.label: AND Blackthorn wins
steps.text: Dragons must beat Violet. A tie does not satisfy this step.

steps.label: AND Mahogany wins
steps.text: Frost must beat Lavender. A tie does not satisfy this step.

steps.label: Playoff berth secured
steps.text: Mt. Silver is in. Johto West and the first seed remain open.

body.text: The reason those favors matter is the limited room left below the division winners. A Reds tie sets a floor of ten wins and a tie. Defeats leave Violet and Lavender at six wins apiece, with five games left and a meeting against each other still to come. Their competing paths, together with Mt. Silver’s head-to-head advantage over Violet and the conference’s other division races, prevent three wild-card clubs from all pushing the Reds out. The half-win counts; replacing either required loss with a tie changes the answer.

If Mt. Silver loses, it cannot clinch this week. If it ties without both favors, it cannot clinch this week either. That means the race remains open, not that the Reds are eliminated. After Olivine, they visit Mahogany, host Saffron, visit Cinnabar and Azalea, then finish at home against Cianwood. Saffron’s Week 15 visit is the obvious next confrontation at the top of the conference.
The games that can rearrange the bracket

Kanto–Johto presently runs Mt. Silver, Blackthorn, Saffron and Cinnabar in the four division positions, followed by Vermilion, Lavender and Olivine. Freeze those seeds and the opening games would be Blackthorn–Olivine, Saffron–Lavender and Cinnabar–Vermilion. Those are possible pairings under an unchanged order, not booked fixtures. Violet is also 6–5 and sits just outside the seven; hosting Blackthorn gives the Falcons an immediate opportunity to change that.

Saffron hosts 7–4 Vermilion after its 35–3 demolition of Cinnabar. A Psi Corps win would widen the Kanto East gap from two wins to three; a Volts win would narrow it to one. Blackthorn follows its trip to Violet with home games against Olivine and Cinnabar before visiting Saffron. Lavender’s next four opponents are Mahogany, Azalea, Celadon and Cerulean, followed by Violet and Blackthorn. The Wails have a chance to build a cushion before two division meetings that could decide how useful that cushion becomes.

Hoenn–Sinnoh currently lines up Mossdeep, Sunyshore, Petalburg, Canalave, Eterna, Dewford and Rustboro. Hold that order and Sunyshore would host Rustboro, Petalburg would host Dewford, and Canalave would host Eterna. Two of those potential opening pairings happen in Week 13: Dewford visits Petalburg, and Canalave visits Eterna. Each gives the contender below the division leader a chance to take ground directly from a rival.

Petalburg is 8–3 and Dewford 7–4, so a Breakers victory would put them level in overall record. Rustboro, now 6–5, hosts 5–6 Mauville; the Stone then visit Fortree and Sunyshore before closing with Canalave, Petalburg and Dewford at home. That closing sequence gives Rustboro substantial control over its own chase, provided it reaches those games close enough to use it. Eterna and Canalave are both 7–4, making their meeting equally relevant to the division and wild-card picture.

For this week’s celebration watch, the instructions are short: Mossdeep has already earned its banner; Mt. Silver earns one by beating Olivine. If the Reds tie, the Blackthorn–Violet and Mahogany–Lavender scoreboards decide whether a playoff place is secured. Everywhere else, Week 13 changes the chase without completing it.

articles.title: Week 13: the rematches have changed
articles.dek: Dewford challenges Petalburg’s home record, Canalave visits Eterna with the division in view, and several familiar opponents arrive with unfamiliar injury problems. Tessa Wren covers all fifteen games.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: Ellis led the Week 12 panel at 11–4. Rowan finished 10–5, I went 9–6, Mara 8–7 and Dorian 4–11. Rowan and Ellis each earned five shared closest-score bonuses; Mara, Dorian and I collected two apiece. My 23–17 Mauville call landed exactly. I would prefer to mention that before anybody asks about Sunyshore.

I asked the Starseekers for 130 rushing yards. They gained forty-five and lost at Eterna. My Saffron key asked for 120 rushing yards and no more than two sacks allowed; the Psi Corps managed ninety-two on the ground and allowed two sacks, then won 35–3. Those are different kinds of misses. The first identified a problem the game exposed. The second overestimated how much running a productive passing attack would need.

Week 13 brings fifteen games and byes for Azalea and Cianwood. Every matchup below is a rematch from the opening three weeks, but the intervening injuries and results have changed the arguments. Dewford at Petalburg gets the separate Game of the Week feature. Canalave at Eterna deserves particular attention as two 7–4 clubs meet in Sinnoh West. The panel’s predictions are opinions saved before the games, and the keys remain checkable after them.

matchups.matchup: Cinnabar needs a working offense before it needs a rebuttal
matchups.analysis: Saffron held Cinnabar to three points, eight rushing yards and 102 through the air. The 7–4 Blaze now visit a 4–7 Viridian team that just lost 7–6. Both defenses have a reasonable invitation to make this unpleasant. Gholdengo's season still contains sixteen touchdown passes, and I expect that broader record to matter more than one dismantling. The Titans won the first meeting 14–10 and can repeat it if Gabite's running gives their defense long rests. Sneasel remains absent, with Toucannon and Bonsly newly carrying three-week absences. Cinnabar has no current multiweek injury absence. Blaine has enough available answers to demand a much cleaner protection performance after eight sacks. I favor the Blaze, without expecting their offense to leap straight back to thirty-eight points.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no more than two sacks and produce two offensive touchdowns.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least 110 yards and hold Cinnabar below twenty points.

matchups.matchup: The Bloom bring a new passing answer to a familiar low-scoring argument
matchups.analysis: Celadon beat Cerulean 34–13 behind Infernape's twenty completions in thirty attempts, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Pewter lost 22–21 despite holding Fuchsia to fifty-nine rushing yards and recording six sacks. The Rockers' own passing produced only sixty-six yards. I narrowly prefer the 3–9 Bloom over the 4–7 hosts because the latest evidence points to a more functional Celadon passing game. Brock can overturn that judgment by giving Delcatty another substantial rushing workload and making Infernape sustain drives without short-field assistance. Pewter won the first meeting 10–7. This time Celadon can bring a little more offense to the discussion, even with Gholdengo, Frosmoth and Anorith still absent.
matchups.awayKey: Complete at least eighteen passes and throw no interceptions.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least one hundred yards and force two takeaways.

matchups.matchup: Fuchsia’s receiver depth meets a defense in retreat
matchups.analysis: Empoleon has thrown for 585 yards across Fuchsia's two straight victories. The latest three touchdowns came with three interceptions, a reminder that improvement and tidiness are different achievements. Sharpedo #89 supplied 114 receiving yards and Manectric 107 against Pewter. Cerulean is 4–7 after four straight losses, most recently allowing Celadon thirty-four points. Farigiraf threw two interceptions. I take the 3–9 Shadows because their receiving production has survived more than one leading target, while the Tide's defense has allowed 248 points. Misty's best answer is to make Fuchsia's protection repeat its six-sack afternoon and convert the resulting field position. Raticate and Vikavolt each remain out two weeks for the hosts; Kleavor remains out six for the visitors.
matchups.awayKey: Gain at least 250 passing yards while throwing no more than one interception.
matchups.homeKey: Record at least four sacks and score twenty-four points.

matchups.matchup: The Volts won the first meeting. This is a less forgiving appointment.
matchups.analysis: Vermilion's 10–9 opening win over Saffron still counts. So do the Psi Corps' latest two results, 52–0 and 35–3. Archam Manning threw for 324 yards at Cinnabar, with HeeDee Lamb catching nine for 177 and two touchdowns. The Volts are 7–4 after winning 7–6 at Viridian; the 9–2 hosts have a considerably more productive offense. Saffron's defensive total is now seventy-three points allowed, and Vermilion managed only thirty-two rushing yards in its latest win. I expect Trent Scarboro's team to make the rematch much less comfortable. Emmitt Smoth remains out one week. Vermilion still has substantial absences, including Delcatty, although Tentacruel's designation has cleared. The Volts need takeaways and a dramatically fuller rushing contribution to keep this within one possession.
matchups.awayKey: Force at least two turnovers and reach ninety rushing yards.
matchups.homeKey: Limit Vermilion to fewer than 250 total yards and score four touchdowns.

matchups.matchup: The Reds answer a loss; Olivine answers an opportunity
matchups.analysis: Mt. Silver is 10–1 after Blackthorn ended its unbeaten run, 30–22. A win over Olivine clinches Johto West and a playoff berth. Tic Thorpe still completed twenty of twenty-eight passes for 260 yards and three touchdowns without an interception. The concern was the support: thirty-seven rushing yards and 358 passing yards allowed. Olivine arrives 6–5 after a 16–3 win over Violet, with five sacks and three Iron Jugulis interceptions. That defense can make the Reds work. I still favor Mt. Silver's more reliable scoring, especially against an Ironclads offense carrying several receiving and backfield absences. Gogoat has one week remaining, Veluza three and Stantler ten. Josh Alakazam remains out ten for the Reds. Jasmine needs a useful ground game; asking Drampa to win a prolonged passing exchange is a harder route.
matchups.awayKey: Allow fewer than one hundred rushing yards and intercept Thorpe at least once.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least 110 yards and hold Olivine below two touchdowns.

matchups.matchup: Blackthorn’s passing test moves from the summit to a division rival
matchups.analysis: Hatterene followed 368 passing yards against Sunyshore with 358 at Mt. Silver, this time turning three touchdown passes into a 30–22 win. Blackthorn is 9–2 and unbeaten in four road games. Violet is 6–5 after its four-game winning streak ended at Olivine, where Iron Jugulis completed ten of thirty with three interceptions. I expect the Dragons to keep exploiting a passing game that now has Seadra and Tinkaton contributing substantial yardage while Ninjask remains absent one week. Furret is newly out two weeks and Grovyle remains out four. The Falcons' earlier 26–20 overtime loss to Blackthorn shows they can make this competitive. Their route requires a much cleaner quarterback performance and fewer possessions handed back to Hatterene.
matchups.awayKey: Complete at least two-thirds of passes and hold Violet below one hundred rushing yards.
matchups.homeKey: Throw no interceptions and convert at least five third downs.

matchups.matchup: Lavender tries to keep the recovery alive without Clanky
matchups.analysis: Two straight wins have moved Lavender to 6–5, but Mr. Clanky is now out two weeks and People Eater five. Frosmoth handled most of the passing in the 18–17 win at Cianwood, while Hobbes ran for 118 yards and Luvdisc caught five passes for sixty-nine. That is a usable foundation against 3–7–1 Mahogany, which rushed for 150 yards and still lost 18–17 at Azalea. I favor the Wails narrowly because their latest win supplied actual evidence of how the available offense can function. Beedrill's injury designation has cleared; his next contribution still has to happen. Exploud gives Pryce a credible running answer, and an early Mahogany lead would test a Lavender passing game operating without its regular quarterback.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for at least 140 yards and hold Lavender below twenty points.
matchups.homeKey: Allow no more than two sacks and gain 120 rushing yards.

matchups.matchup: Mauville finds the Stone at an awkward moment
matchups.analysis: Rustboro's 35–7 defeat to Mossdeep cost it more than a winning streak: My Way, Son is now out six weeks. Philly ran for sixty-one yards, but Porygon-Z completed seven of seventeen for ninety-nine after throwing five touchdowns in the previous game. Mauville is 5–6 after two straight wins, with Togekiss throwing for 274 yards and two scores against Fortree. I pick the visitors to bring Rustboro back to .500 because their current passing has fewer repairs to make. The 6–5 Stone can reverse that forecast through Philly and a renewed connection to Gibby Timmy, who still produced seventy-four receiving yards against Mossdeep. Mauville's first meeting was a 23–0 win; Tyler Scarboro has a very specific result to improve upon.
matchups.awayKey: Gain at least 250 passing yards and finish three touchdown drives.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least 130 yards and hold Mauville below twenty-four points.

matchups.matchup: Game of the Week: the division lead meets the traveling Breakers
matchups.analysis: Petalburg is 8–3, 5–0 at home and one game ahead of 7–4 Dewford. The Breakers have won four straight and four of five road games. A visitor win levels their records; a Pride win makes the gap two. Norman's offense has found enough scoring even when the passing is sparse: Iron Valiant completed seven of twenty-one for 116 yards in a 21–18 win over Sootopolis. Dewford beat Lavaridge 22–16 with 105 passing yards and eighty-four rushing. I give Petalburg a field-goal edge because its defense has allowed less rushing production across the season and Oinkologne supplies a steadier foundation for ordinary possessions. Brawly's route is to protect Frosmoth and make the hosts settle for kicks. Petalburg won the first meeting 19–12. Nobody should assume the rematch will be comfortable.
matchups.awayKey: Commit no turnovers and hold Petalburg below one hundred rushing yards.
matchups.homeKey: Complete at least half of pass attempts and allow no more than two touchdowns.

matchups.matchup: Two offenses adjust, one without its leading target
matchups.analysis: Sootopolis produced 260 passing yards and still lost 21–18 at Petalburg. Arbok, who scored the receiving touchdown, is now listed out seventeen weeks. Heatmor remains out two. Lavaridge lost 22–16 at Dewford despite Delphox's 204 yards and two touchdowns; two interceptions weakened that contribution. Both clubs are 4–7. I favor the Inferno at home because Delphox still has a clearer set of recent receiving answers, including Maractus and his sixty-one yards against the Breakers. Stantler remains absent one week, so Cranidos' sixty-five rushing yards matter as more than a supporting detail. Wallace can win the rematch by keeping Rillaboom productive and spreading targets beyond the missing Arbok. The Surge won 17–10 in Week 1; their offense now has a substantial new question.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for at least ninety yards and complete passes to five receivers.
matchups.homeKey: Throw no interceptions and score touchdowns on three possessions.

matchups.matchup: Mossdeep’s next backfield must carry an unbeaten record
matchups.analysis: The Eclipse have clinched Hoenn East and are 11–0 after beating Rustboro 35–7, with Dram Marino throwing five touchdowns on seventeen attempts. Ninjulio Jones caught three. Now Ninjaskamara is out four weeks and Richard Furman five, alongside Marshall Flock's remaining three. Poury Holt's eighty-two rushing yards at Rustboro are therefore immediately relevant. Fortree is 3–8 after losing 23–17 at Mauville, but Rabsca's 242 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions supplied a substantial improvement over the Saffron shutout. I expect Mossdeep's passing and defensive pressure to carry the day. Winona's route is to make the new rushing distribution inefficient and force long conversions without handing Marino short fields. Pawmot remains out five weeks. Fortree cannot afford to add to the thirty-nine sacks it has already allowed.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no more than two sacks and score four offensive touchdowns.
matchups.homeKey: Hold Mossdeep below 120 rushing yards and lose no turnovers.

matchups.matchup: Snowpoint brings its best recent finishing to a low-margin rematch
matchups.analysis: The Blizzard beat Veilstone 24–6, with Drampa completing twenty-four of thirty-one for 220 yards and Abomasnow catching eight for eighty-eight. Oreburgh lost 10–9 to Pastoria after Cryogonal threw two interceptions. Snowpoint is 3–8 and Oreburgh 3–9; neither has room for the helpful giveaway. I take Candice's visitors because the latest passing performance converted reliable completions into a better scoring total. The concern is travel: Snowpoint has lost all four road games. Diggersby's running can give the Miners a slower, more manageable contest, but Huntail is newly out two weeks. The Blizzard won the opening meeting 20–13. Repeating it away from home would make this latest improvement more convincing.
matchups.awayKey: Complete at least sixty-five percent of passes and score two offensive touchdowns.
matchups.homeKey: Throw no interceptions and rush for at least ninety yards.

matchups.matchup: A shared record, a division rematch, and very little spare scoring
matchups.analysis: Both clubs are 7–4, with Canalave holding first place in Sinnoh West and Eterna immediately behind. The Bulwark won their opening meeting 10–6. Now they return from a bye to face a team that just held Sunyshore to six points and forty-five rushing yards. Tatsugiri completed eighteen of twenty-five for 180 yards and two touchdowns in Eterna's 14–6 win. I favor Gardenia's hosts because that passing answer gives their defense a more useful partner than Canalave's recent offense has provided. Byron's last result was 6–3 at Olivine. Gabite's 741 season rushing yards offer the visitors a credible way to make the game smaller, but Eterna has allowed only 663 rushing yards all season. Kecleon remains out two weeks and Octillery four for Canalave. The Thorns have no current injury absence.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for at least 120 yards and hold Eterna below fourteen points.
matchups.homeKey: Gain at least 160 passing yards and allow no more than one touchdown.

matchups.matchup: Sunyshore has to turn receiving yards back into points
matchups.analysis: Scol Alexander caught six passes for 176 yards and a touchdown at Eterna. Sunyshore still lost 14–6 because the rest of the scoring operation failed to keep pace. The 8–3 Starseekers now visit a rested 3–7–1 Hearthome side whose last appearance was a 24–6 loss to Violet. I expect the visitors to restore a rushing contribution after managing only forty-five yards against the Thorns. Myles Gabite remains absent one week, while Hearthome still lacks Luxray, Sunflora and Mr. Mime. Fantina can challenge this forecast if Frosmoth avoids the interceptions that damaged the last game and the defense makes Sunyshore repeatedly earn short gains. The Starseekers won the first meeting 28–3. Karson Jones needs a convincing finish, not another impressive receiver total standing beside six points.
matchups.awayKey: Rush for at least 120 yards and finish three touchdown drives.
matchups.homeKey: Throw no interceptions and hold Sunyshore below twenty-four points.

matchups.matchup: Pastoria’s third straight win meets Veilstone’s other address
matchups.analysis: The Waves won 10–9 at Oreburgh despite two Farigiraf interceptions, extending their run to three victories and reaching 5–6. Veilstone has lost four straight and is 4–8, but the location matters: the Fists are 4–1 at home and 0–7 away. I still narrowly favor Pastoria because its recent defense has kept limited scoring sufficient, and Watchog #58's running gives the offense a manageable assignment. Arbok remains out three weeks and Oinkologne two. Maylene needs Tatsugiri's passing to produce touchdowns after a six-point afternoon in Snowpoint. The first meeting ended 7–0 to Pastoria. A rematch with a similarly small margin would suit the Waves, provided they stop supplying free chances through the air.
matchups.awayKey: Allow no more than one touchdown and throw no interceptions.
matchups.homeKey: Rush for at least ninety yards and score on three possessions.
